This is because on Windows and Mac they tend to write their own drivers. So if their hardware's API does not comply with standards, they don't care as they can code around it within their own drivers.

Additionally, sometimes vendors have relationships with Apple and/or Microsoft which means they purposely create a fast and slow set of hardware APIs. Yes, generally speaking the difference is in the hardware and associated drivers.

But... this can get a big more complicated because of OS differences and things like hibernation. Linux attempts to maximize memory use whereas Windows does not. Additionally, Linux and Windows have very different paging strategies. On Windows, by default, all pages are backed by the paging file. This means that during hibernation it needs to persist a smaller amount of memory as the paged pages are already persistent within the paging file. Window's method also has a couple of other advantages, but they are generally corner cases whereby for most workloads Linux's paging activity is superior and open to dramatically better tuning opportunities. Yet the fact remains, Windows does have a slight hibernation performance advantage, including in wakeup.

Long story short, as long as the hardware vendor implements standards compliant hardware, there should be no significant differences in sleep/suspend. There may, however, be slight differences in hibernation, depending on the memory nature of certain workloads.
